source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: Eight LLMs tested on cognitive-map and planning tasks built from human experiments (graphs, shortcuts, detours, reward and policy revaluation). No evidence of out-of-the-box cognitive maps or planning.
numbers: Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, davinci-003, Claude-1, Bard, Cohere, LLaMA-13B, Alpaca-7B (plus Pythia-20B in tables). Each condition run 30 times for OpenAI models; all factors (LLM, graph, domain, task, temperature) significant in regression.
quote: These findings do not support the idea of emergent out-of-the-box planning ability in LLMs.
limits: Closed models, architecture and training data unknown; text-only; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: S2 map cannot be assumed: the model will not build a reliable state-move map by itself. It must be written explicitly.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: Performance falls as the task needs more multi-step use of the graph. Simple one-step tasks are near ceiling for GPT-4, multi-step and revaluation tasks are poor.
numbers: Mean score (Table 3, GPT-4-32k): 1-step path 0.99, 2-step 0.82, 3-step 0.55, n-step 0.47, policy revaluation 0.21, reward revaluation 0.67, transition revaluation 0.60. Bard 1-step 0.05; LLaMA-13B 1-step 0.23.
limits: Score is a task-specific metric; policy revaluation is very low across all models (best 0.28, Claude-1).
agent_relevance: Check the map step by step; one-step edge lookup is reliable, multi-hop chaining and policy change are not. Use per-step verification rather than trusting long paths.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: Three failure modes on community-structured graphs: hallucinated edges, longer-than-shortest routes, and loops. Models list edges correctly as (state, action, state) tuples yet fail to use them.
numbers: Shortest path to a state one cluster away: GPT-4 success 0 of 30 at temperature 0; never above 10% at temperature 0.5 or 1.
limits: Dense-community graphs only; one prompt family.
agent_relevance: Knowing the edge list is not the same as using the map. Add an explicit check that each step is an edge in the stored list, and loop detection (visited set).

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: Graph-search instructions in the prompt (BFS or DFS, explained at high level) helped GPT-4 on several community-graph tasks but not all. Gains depend on temperature.
numbers: Experiment 2: 30 runs per prompt and temperature. BFS or DFS improved cluster counting at temperature 0 and 0.5 but less at 1; within-cluster shortest path improved at all temperatures (BFS best at 0); one-cluster-away path improved only with BFS at 0.5. CoT shortcut tasks: GPT-4 1.00 (non-teleporting), 0.50 (teleporting).
limits: Effects inconsistent; no paired effect sizes in main text; one model.
agent_relevance: A named search procedure in the scaffold helps some tasks; it is a partial fix, so pair it with checks.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: LLMs do better when full trajectories are in the prompt and the graph is sparse; node count alone does not explain difficulty, cluster connectivity does.
numbers: The 15-node, 3-dense-cluster graph was often worse than the 16-node, 4-cluster graph that had better cross-cluster links.
limits: Observation, not a controlled manipulation.
agent_relevance: Keep the map sparse and local (only the relevant subgraph); do not dump a large dense graph.

source: Kim et al. (2024) How Language Models Extrapolate Outside the Training Data: A Case Study in Textualized Gridworld
finding: Cognitive-map chain of thought (build the map by marking visited cells, then plan from it) lets a trained model extrapolate to larger unseen grids far better than plain next-token or ordinary CoT.
numbers: Optimal-plan rate: implicit baseline 19.0%, best explicit CoT 26.5%, cognitive map (backward, unmark) 76.5%. Reachable-plan rate: 32.1%, 33.9%, 88.5% (backward mark). Above 40% success at complexity 25 versus training max 15.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, small gridworld, text only.
agent_relevance: Supports S2: an explicit map built before planning beats planning directly, but here the effect comes from training.

source: Kim et al. (2024) How Language Models Extrapolate Outside the Training Data: A Case Study in Textualized Gridworld
finding: The cognitive-map format could NOT be induced by prompting. Frontier models given few-shot examples scored near zero.
numbers: 0, 1, 2, 4-shot: Llama 3 8B, 70B and GPT-4o 0% in baseline prompting; GPT-o1 reached up to 38% with 4-shot plain prompting (not map prompting). Authors say map reasoning needs gradient training.
quote: cannot be induced through simple prompting
limits: PDF table layout partly garbled; only the authors' map format tested.
agent_relevance: A prompt alone may not make a model build a good map in this format. Test whether our S2 prompt really changes behaviour.

source: Kim et al. (2024) How Language Models Extrapolate Outside the Training Data: A Case Study in Textualized Gridworld
finding: Online exploration (DFS) beats offline map planning on reachability.
numbers: DFS 94.5% reachable success versus 88.5% for cognitive map (BWD MARK). Ablation: backtracking in forward construction raised 42.3% to 85.2%.
limits: Single environment family.
agent_relevance: Offline map plus a fallback of explicit search is a sensible pair (S2 then search operator).

source: Gurnee & Tegmark (2024) Language Models Represent Space and Time
finding: Linear probes read real-world coordinates (latitude, longitude, year) from Llama-2 hidden layers. The model holds a map-like code for places and times.
numbers: Out-of-sample R2 at 60% depth, Llama-2-70b linear: world 0.911, USA 0.864, NYC 0.359, historical figures 0.835, entertainment 0.885, headlines 0.746. Llama-2-7b world 0.881.
quote: LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales.
limits: Probes are supervised; NYC is much weaker. R2 shows the information is there, not that the model uses it for planning.
agent_relevance: LLMs hold a world-geometry prior from pretraining; the S2 map can lean on that for known places but not for novel task graphs.

source: Gurnee & Tegmark (2024) Language Models Represent Space and Time
finding: Held-out generalisation is weaker: probes place held-out countries in the right relative position but not absolute position. MLP probes add little over linear.
numbers: Proximity error (random 0.5), world dataset: 0.071 nominal vs 0.164 held out; NYC 0.262 vs 0.433. Linear vs MLP R2 for world 0.911 vs 0.926 (table rows partly garbled in PDF text).
limits: Authors call it weak evidence for real features versus a memorised mapping.
agent_relevance: A decodable map does not prove a usable one.

source: Gurnee & Tegmark (2024) Language Models Represent Space and Time
finding: Individual space neurons and time neurons were found; representations are robust to prompt variants and shared across entity types.
numbers: Llama-2 7B, 13B, 70B; six datasets; layer-wise sweeps.
limits: Only Llama-2; no causal test on planning.
agent_relevance: Use the model as a source of spatial priors, not as the place to store the task map.

source: Whittington, Warren & Behrens (2022) Relating Transformers to Models and Neural Representations of the Hippocampal Formation
finding: A transformer with recurrent position encodings reproduces grid-like and place-like units, and is mathematically close to the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine (TEM).
numbers: TEM-t learns grid cells and has memory neurons that remap randomly across environments like place cells; far more sample efficient than TEM, which takes up to 50,000 gradient updates (stopped at 20,000 here).
limits: Authors say the TEM comparison is not fully fair (TEM code not tuned for speed). Simulation, not recordings.
agent_relevance: Attention over past (state, action) memory acts like a map-building hippocampus. Argues for writing the (state, move) memory into context.

source: Li et al. (2023) Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task (Othello-GPT)
finding: A GPT trained only on Othello move text builds an internal board-state representation that is causally used for next moves.
numbers: Illegal-move error rate 0.01% (synthetic-trained), 5.17% (championship-trained), 93.29% untrained. Linear probes error never below 20%; nonlinear probes much lower; interventions change predictions.
limits: Toy game with exact rules; later linear-representation follow-ups not opened here.
agent_relevance: A sequence model can learn a world map from moves alone; a prompted LLM on a new task cannot be assumed to.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Asking the model to draw the state after each step (text grid) improves spatial navigation and tiling versus plain CoT. This is a prompt-level map.
numbers: Natural-language navigation: VoT beats GPT-4 without visualisation by 23.5%. Sets: 200 3x3 maps (language nav); 496 maps with 2520 QA (visual nav). Significance p<0.05 vs all baselines except p<0.16 vs CoT in language navigation.
quote: VoT significantly enhances the spatial reasoning abilities of LLMs.
limits: Only GPT-4/4V; gain modest versus CoT in language navigation; Table 1 values garbled in PDF text.
agent_relevance: Strong fit for S2: have the agent redraw the map after each move. Cheap prompt-only method.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in LLMs
finding: The drawn state is often wrong even when the final answer is right. Visualisation accuracy is the weak link.
numbers: Table 2: compliance with spatial constraints about 51-52%; state-visualisation accuracy only 24-26%; correct decisions in 65-77% of cases when the visualisation was accurate. Ring task: GPT-4 CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5% (n=200).
limits: Visual navigation and tiling only.
agent_relevance: A map the model writes needs verification against the rules. Add a check on each redraw.

source: Park et al. (2025) ICLR: In-Context Learning of Representations
finding: Given random-walk traces over a graph (grid, ring, hex) whose nodes are ordinary words, Llama-3.1-8B reorganises its hidden representations to mirror the graph as context grows.
numbers: Square grid, ring, hexagonal grid; sudden re-organisation as context length rises (Fig. 1, 400 vs 1400 tokens); Dirichlet energy over the true graph falls with context; model predicts valid next nodes with non-trivial accuracy.
quote: there is a sudden re-organization from pretrained semantic representations to in-context representations aligned with the graph structure
limits: Small open model; toy graphs; pretrained semantics compete with context structure.
agent_relevance: In-context structure learning is real but needs many examples. For S2, give long consistent traces or state the graph outright.

source: Park et al. (2025) ICLR: In-Context Learning of Representations
finding: When the new graph conflicts with strong pretraining semantics (days of the week), both structures coexist; the in-context one appears in other principal components.
numbers: 7-node ring: original semantic ring in first PCs, new ring in PCs 3-4; in-context accuracy in Fig. 14.
limits: Interpretation by PCA visualisation.
agent_relevance: Task graphs that clash with common-sense meaning are harder; use neutral node labels.

source: Ding et al. (2024) MANGO: A Benchmark for Evaluating Mapping and Navigation Abilities of LLMs
finding: 53 text-game mazes with walkthroughs; hundreds of route-finding (RF) and destination-finding (DF) questions each. GPT-4 is best but weak on routes.
numbers: GPT-4 answers only about half of RF questions; humans answered perfectly on sampled questions. Human eval (Table 2): RF success 0.82 (n=31), DF 1.00 (n=30). Models: RWKV, Llama-2, Claude-1/2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4.
limits: Jericho text games; humans were the student authors; contamination of famous games possible.
agent_relevance: Reading a walkthrough does not give a map. Convert experience to an explicit graph, then query it.

source: Ding et al. (2024) MANGO: A Benchmark for Evaluating Mapping and Navigation Abilities of LLMs
finding: Better mapping and navigation helps downstream text-game play. A pipeline that maps a walkthrough to a symbolic graph and then searches was tried and found very challenging.
numbers: GPT-4 significantly beats GPT-3.5 on shared questions (pairwise tables); appendix C.4 holds the graph-then-search results (numbers not extracted).
limits: Pipeline numbers not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Map extraction, not map search, is the bottleneck; invest in the extraction step.

source: Einarsson (2025) MazeEval: A Benchmark for Testing Sequential Decision-Making in Language Models
finding: Coordinate-only maze navigation (5x5 to 15x15) with function calls. One reasoning model is perfect; the others collapse past 9x9, and all those failures are loops.
numbers: O3 perfect up to 30x30; others fail beyond 9x9 with 100% of failures from revisiting a cell at least 10 times. Max size English vs Icelandic: Claude Opus 4 11 vs 8, Claude Sonnet 4 12 vs 8. Icelandic gap W=273, p<0.001, d=0.50; Opus 4 p=0.016, d=0.96. Wall hits spiked to 17.2 average in 9x9 Icelandic.
limits: Eight models, five mazes per size; coordinate feedback only.
agent_relevance: Looping is the main failure: keep an explicit visited set in the map. Reasoning-trained models may build a map internally.

source: Baumgartner et al. (2025) Cognitive Maps in Language Models: A Mechanistic Analysis of Spatial Planning
finding: GPT-2 trained on random-walk (exploration) data builds a map-like internal coordinate system; models trained only on shortest paths learn a path-dependent heuristic.
numbers: Foraging model direction-token ablation: near zero when ablating early layers, 100% from layer 8 (sharp phase transition). Shortest-path models stay dependent on direction tokens across all 12 layers. Next-step accuracy 100% at 2-3 steps, 71% near 11 steps, over 96% beyond 30. SP-Hamiltonian 100% in-distribution but 0% elsewhere; SP-Random-Walk over 97%.
quote: map-like representation of space, akin to a cognitive map
limits: Small GPT-2 trained from scratch on grids; not a prompted LLM.
agent_relevance: Exploration data teaches a map; goal-only data teaches shortcuts. Suggests the agent should explore and record before planning.

source: Baumgartner et al. (2025) Cognitive Maps in Language Models: A Mechanistic Analysis of Spatial Planning
finding: Path-dependent planners generalise poorly to longer path lengths.
numbers: Shortest-path accuracy falls from 95% at Manhattan distance 1 to 22% at 8 (SP-RW); SP-Hamiltonian 83% at distance 1 to 0% by 7.
limits: Training-regime specific.
agent_relevance: Do not trust goal-trained behaviour beyond the tested path length.

source: Bugaud (2026) CheeseBench: Evaluating LLMs on Rodent Behavioral Neuroscience Paradigms
finding: Thirteen LLMs on nine rodent paradigms (Morris water maze, Barnes, T-maze, radial arm, etc.) as ASCII gridworlds with no task instructions. The best frontier model matches the rodent reference.
numbers: Claude Opus 4.7 86.7% average vs approximate rodent 78.9%, random 38.0%; best open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-7B 68.0%, 32B 64.7%, 72B 58.5%; tabular Q-learning 31.2%.
limits: Rodent baselines approximate and from varied protocols; the same model ranged 20% to 57% by interface parameters alone.
agent_relevance: Interface choices matter as much as the model; measure scaffolds on this style of test.

source: Bugaud (2026) CheeseBench: Evaluating LLMs on Rodent Behavioral Neuroscience Paradigms
finding: Chain-of-thought prompting and longer history hurt; open-weight models fail the working-memory radial arm maze.
numbers: Qwen2.5-VL-7B ablation: default 46.7%, CoT 31.9%, minimal 35.6%, few-shot 29.6%. Radial arm maze: best open-weight 10.0% vs rodent 70%. Spatial learning (Morris, Barnes, Star) average 57%.
limits: Ablation on one small model.
agent_relevance: Generic CoT is not a map; prefer structured state tracking and short history.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: Using the LLM as a world model (predict the next state after an action) plus Monte Carlo tree search beats CoT in Blocksworld.
numbers: Blocksworld success, LLaMA-33B: CoT 0.17, 0.02, 0.00 at 2-, 4-, 6-step; RAP(10) 1.00, 0.86, 0.26; RAP(20) 1.00, 0.88, 0.42. CoT with GPT-4: 0.50, 0.63, 0.40. Average success 64%; 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT.
limits: Many model calls; 6-step still low; the world-model step is an LLM prediction that can err.
agent_relevance: Explicit state-after-action predictions plus search is a tested scaffold for S2 into search.
